text.p: Contract talks between Continental Airlines Inc and its pilots will continue beyond the airline's optimistic July 1 target date, but "negotiations continue to go well," the airline said.

Continental originally aimed to complete negotiations by the time the pilots' current contract becomes amendable on June 30. But Jim Moody, a spokesman for the pilots union said that "was a bit of an impossible goal due to the complex nature of the contract."
Instead the pilots believe it is "probably feasible" to complete negotiations by October 1, Moody said.
Labor experts said the talks appear to be progressing smoothly, with both sides maneuvering for position, but still showing a willingness to continue active negotiations.
Even if the talks lasted until the fall, that would be relatively fast in an industry where contract negotiations often linger for years, labor experts said.

The pilots union maintains that it is "still requiring, not asking, but requiring an industry standard wage and retirement package," said Independent Association of Continental Pilots president Len Nikolai.

Earlier this month, Continental said the pilot's demands would cost $1.4 billion over three years, which "would end this era of profitability and plunge us back into the crisis mode that we have only recently escaped."

The union said the company's assessment that the union demands would cost $1.4 billion over three years is "pretty accurate." But the union said their proposal would not put the company in a financial crisis.
"It's a matter of priorities," Nikolai said.

The union said Continental, tha nation's fifth largest airline, has found money for other investments, such as plans to buy $3 billion worth of aircraft over the next 20 years, plans to buy the rest of its Air Micronesia subsidiary for about $73 million and recent advertising promotions.
"Expenditures of that kind are probably good business, but it's also good business to pay your employees industry-standard wages," Nikolai said.

Continental's recent investment in facilities and fleet improvement are signs of the airline's vibrancy, which is positive for all of its employees, analysts said. Continental remains one of the industry's most successful turnaround stories, posting record profits and winning several top performance awards since it emerged from bankruptcy in 1993.

"The pilots had been complaining for years that the company was so mismanaged, that they couldn't buy planes and that there was no plan for the future of the company. That's all changed, said Edward Starkman, an airline analyst with Dillon Read. "Buying airplanes is always good for pilots," Starkman said.

The two sides continued negotiations this week, but negotiators, who are working with a federal mediator, will take a break next week for the Fourth of July holiday, the company said. Negotiations began April 2.
The main issues currently under consideration are staffing, hours of service and scheduling, the union said.
The pilots "would like to successfully conclude these issues before moving on to the more difficult economic items," the union said in a recorded message to its members.
Analysts said that Continental management may be amenable to pay increases but could resist demands over the size of the increases.
"You have a management team coming to the table willing, or even looking forward to increasing wages. But that dosen't mean you're going to give away your recent profitability," Starkman said.

Continental is just one of several major airlines in labor talks. But the Houston-based carrier is in a much stronger financial position and has better labor relations than some other airlines currently in negotiations, analysts said.
Meanwhile, Trans World Airlines Inc, which lost $71.6 million in the first quarter, recently opened talks with its pilots.

Pilots at Northwest Airlines Corp said its union leaders are considering applying for federal mediation. Northwest's pilots said progress has been slow, but agreements have been reached on two minor sections of the contract.

Also, US Airways Group Inc has struggled with labor negotiations since the pilot's contract became amendable on April 30, 1996. The airline said since it has yet to reach a cost-cutting pact with it unionized employees, it must focus on being a smaller, regional carrier.
